data.title: Beckov – a Slavic hillfort on the castle crag above the Váh
data.excerpt: In Slovak legend, Beckov castle is bound up with the magnate Štibor of Štiborice, who is even said to have had it built for his jester. In fact the castle crag above the Váh was occupied far earlier: people lived on this exceptionally strategic site in the Late La Tène and Roman periods, and in the second half of the 9th century a Slavic hillfort was built there, guarding access to the Trenčín centre.
data.metaTitle: Beckov – a Slavic hillfort above the Váh
data.metaDescription: Beckov's crag above the Váh was occupied from prehistory through the La Tène and Roman periods to an early medieval Slavic hillfort. Plus the legend of Štibor.

children.text: The Slavs on the castle crag of Beckov

In the original Slovak legends, Beckov castle is linked with the name of Štibor of Štiborice (also Ctibor of Ctiborice, or Stibor of Stiborice). According to one of them this prominent magnate even had it built for his jester, in return for his devotion and faithful service, after he had entertained the guests exceedingly well on one of the hunts. In reality the Beckov castle crag was already occupied in prehistoric times. People lived on this strategically exceptional site as early as the Late La Tène period and in the Roman period, and later an early medieval Slavic hillfort was built on it.

The castle crag stands in the village of Beckov, which spreads out on the eastern side of the Váh, north-east of Nové Mesto nad Váhom and south-west of Trenčín, a town wrapped in legend. The early medieval settlement lay on a rocky eminence. It was built on the site where, in the later periods of the Middle Ages, a stone castle was erected. The beginnings of the stone castle reach back to the 13th century at the latest, and its remains now rise above the village. It follows from this that Beckov castle was not built by Štibor of Štiborice. He received it from the Hungarian king Sigismund of Luxembourg in 1388. It is with this man, however, that the most important period in the castle's history is connected, when he was a favoured magnate of King Sigismund. Štibor of Štiborice was a Pole by origin and belonged among the wealthiest oligarchs in the Kingdom of Hungary of that time. He owned approximately 18 castles and around 300 villages, and he always sought to defend the interests of King Sigismund.
THE SIGNIFICANCE OF THE SLAVIC HILLFORT

This site was systematically excavated under the direction of M. Kodoňová and Š. Tóthová, staff of the Monuments Institute of the Slovak Republic. The early medieval fortified Slavic settlement, one of the strategic and military watch points in the Váh region, was most probably established in the second half of the 9th century. It extended over approximately the whole area of the later medieval castle of the 13th–18th centuries, covering 1.45 ha, with the highest elevation in the north-western part of the crag — 253 m. This fact does not yet entirely correspond with the preceding Late La Tène (Late Celtic) and Early Roman occupation, which clearly exceeded the dimensions of the area taken up by the stone castle. The area of this prehistoric occupation covered as much as 2.5 ha of the rocky eminence.

During the rule of the Slavs the early medieval hillfort was not a more significant political and social centre. The fortified settlement at Beckov had above all an important military and watch function thanks to its good strategic position, which was exploited to a corresponding degree in later periods as well. It served as an exceptional fortress protecting access to the area administered by the „Trenčín“ early medieval territorial-administrative centre in the Great Moravian and post-Great Moravian periods. This Great Moravian territorial unit of Trenčín continuously formed the basis of the castellany of „Trecen“, the future Trenčín comitatus in the Kingdom of Hungary. The hillfort at Beckov was thus an advanced watch point of the central fortified settlement at Trenčín — a manorial court administered by a Great Moravian magnate.

Finds of pottery and the remains of dwelling features also confirm that an early medieval Slavic upland settlement stood here, its beginnings reaching into the second half of the 9th and the first half of the 10th century. The upland and most probably fortified settlement came into being here in the Great Moravian period. The continuity of occupation clearly persisted here from the Great Moravian period through the post-Great Moravian period, the Hungarian invasion and the beginnings of the Hungarian state up to the demise of the castle at the beginning of the 18th century. It is precisely with the post-Great Moravian chronological horizon that we may connect the account of the chronicler of Béla III, magister P., the so-called Anonymus. It dates from the turn of the 12th and 13th centuries and speaks of the capture of the castles of Šintava, Hlohovec, Trenčín, Bana and Blundus by Old Hungarian war bands at the time of their arrival in the Carpathian Basin. By means of a linguistic interpretation of the Hungarian name for Beckov — „Blondóc“ — we may identify the castrum Blundus mentioned in Anonymus's chronicle with the rocky promontory of Beckov with its Great Moravian and post-Great Moravian upland settlement, where the castle of the 13th–18th centuries later arose. This interpretation is at present more or less confirmed, thanks also to the latest results of the most recent archaeological excavation. It is demonstrated by the quantity of finds from the Great Moravian and post-Great Moravian periods, which indirectly testify that a fortified settlement existed here at that time. Blundus may therefore be connected with the castle eminence at Beckov. Anonymus's account of the capture of the „castrorum“ of Trenčín and Beckov is, however, not founded on truth, because Old Hungarian military groups reached with their northern incursions, as late as 930 – 940, at most the northern line Bratislava – Hlohovec – Nitra – Levice – Rimavská Sobota. It was strategically disadvantageous for them to go into the valley of the middle Váh region, surrounded by the Považský Inovec and the White Carpathians. This assertion is supported also by the fact that the greater part of the Váh lowland — the future southern part of the Trenčín comitatus — was actually taken into the emerging Hungarian state probably only during the reign of King Ladislaus I (1077 – 1095). Even though, in formal territorial-administrative terms, it had been part of the Kingdom of Hungary since 1017, under the reign of Stephen I (1000 – 1038). The refutation of this interpretation of Anonymus too, concerning the capture of Slavic hillforts by Hungarian nomadic warriors, only demonstrates the long-known unreliability of this source.

This is confirmed also by the find situation at the Slavic magnate's residence at Ducové near Piešťany, which lies south of Beckov. For there we can date the distinct traces of its capture as late as the second half of the 10th century, and not to an immediate demise following the fall of Great Moravia. Beckov, moreover, lies considerably further north than Ducové and thus in territory less attractive to the nomadic population.

The poorly preserved find situation did not allow the fortifications of the 9th or possibly the 10th–11th centuries to be identified more closely, but, according to the authors of the excavation, we may hypothetically place them in the area of the later so-called lower castle of the 13th–18th centuries. The advantageous position itself in terms of terrain — a rocky promontory protected on the north-western side by an almost insurmountable rock crag — fairly speaks of the strategic, military and watch function of the site. In spite of these facts, it nevertheless remains veiled in mystery, and not only in connection with the Middle Ages but also with prehistory. These lines clearly confirm the important strategic standing of the rocky castle crag of Beckov among the Slavic hillforts in the territory of present-day Slovakia. The significance of this site in the Early Middle Ages is underlined also by the fact that we know of further Slavic sites in the cadastral area of the village of Beckov.

As for the other archaeological finds from the area of Beckov, mention must be made of the discovery of a settlement in the Sady district — Prague-type pottery from the period between the end of the 5th and the middle of the 7th century, from the time when the Slavic population was penetrating the region. A residential semi-sunken building with an oven whose dome was built of quarry stone was found here, and the pottery was handmade. The second find dates from the end of the 7th and the beginning of the 8th century — a pit and a well 295 cm deep and 205 cm in diameter; and the third find is from the turn of the 9th and 10th centuries — 8 features (a semi-sunken building and settlement pits with pottery finds).(6) The archaeological excavation of Beckov castle confirmed the existence of an advanced Great Moravian settlement on the castle rock, with a rich assemblage of pottery finds(7). At a locality south-west of the agricultural co-operative a destroyed Slavic hamlet was found in 1975(8). Remains of semi-sunken buildings, pottery, an iron knife and a lost sword were also found in the village itself, in Slnečná and Zelená streets. Behind the rocks, „za skalicami“, evidence of occupation from the 10th century was found in 1983.
